findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an acceptance criterion / assert in the regression test that the emitted timestamp round-trips to the exact stored value (int(wire_value) == stored_value), not merely that no serialization error occurs.
evidence: Fix shape: 'so int(wire_value) == stored_value with no rounding'
Root cause: 'the value silently truncates (no error): stored 1787856371950409998 reads back as 1787856371950410000'
AC: 'returns a ticket list with no serialization error. Verify: the tool call returns a well-formed result.'
findings.finding: No acceptance criterion verifies that the timestamp value round-trips exactly (int(wire_value) == stored_value with no rounding). The ACs only check 'no serialization error', but the plan's own root cause identifies silent truncation (1787856371950409998 -> 1787856371950410000) as the more dangerous failure mode for plain-JSON.parse clients. A fix that stringifies could pass every 'no error' AC while still not being verified to preserve the exact value.
scenarios: A regression that stringifies but loses a digit passes the 'no error' ACs; the corruption path is never asserted against.
findings.suggested_fix: In the regression test AC, assert the exact-value contract: parse the wire timestamp, int()-convert, and assert equality with the stored time_ns value (e.g. the 19-digit integer is preserved exactly).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a criterion/test that exercises a ticket carrying comments/attestations/signature timestamps (and show_ticket) so the nested list[dict] timestamp fields the root cause names are proven fixed.
evidence: 'More ride in raw list[dict] fields: comments[].timestamp, attestations.<kind>.signed_at, signature.signed_at.'
'show_ticket 2' integers measured
ACs cover only list_tickets and ready_tickets
findings.finding: The root cause names show_ticket (2 integers) and nested raw list[dict] fields (comments[].timestamp, attestations.<kind>.signed_at, signature.signed_at) as carriers of the hazard, but no acceptance criterion exercises show_ticket or a ticket that actually contains comments/attestations/signature. The fix is described as applying 'at the MCP tool-return seam only' generically, yet the ACs only exercise list_tickets and ready_tickets.
findings.location: Root cause 'The changeable artifacts' / Acceptance criteria
scenarios: A seam guard that only rewrites declared model fields but not nested list[dict] values would leave comments[].timestamp broken, uncaught by any AC.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the regression test to include a ticket with at least one comment and an attestation/signature, and assert those nested signed_at/timestamp values also round-trip exactly.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Strengthen the regression-test AC to assert the exact stored timestamp round-trips losslessly (parse the wire value back and require int(wire_value) == stored time.time_ns() value), not merely that no serialization error is raised.
evidence: 'the test exists, fails when the guard is disabled, and passes with it enabled'
Root cause: 'stored 1787856371950409998 reads back as 1787856371950410000. This is why the tool "worked" from Claude Code while quietly corrupting data.'
Fix shape: 'int(wire_value) == stored_value with no rounding'
findings.finding: The regression-test acceptance criterion asserts only 'no serialization error' / 'returns a ticket list', not that the out-of-range timestamp survives losslessly (int(wire_value) == stored_value). A fix that emits a lossy/truncated value — or a test that snapshots current output — could pass this criterion while silently corrupting data, which is the exact silent-truncation failure mode the root-cause section documents for plain JSON.parse clients.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria — 'An MCP-layer regression test exercises list_tickets... fails when the guard is disabled'
scenarios: A guard that emits a truncated or approximated string passes the 'no error' test but still corrupts the timestamp — the same silent data loss the plan attributes to the other client.
A change-detector test that snapshots whatever the fixed code emits locks in whatever value is produced without proving lossless round-trip.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the test AC: the test must parse the emitted string field and assert equality with the original 19-digit stored integer, covering a value strictly greater than 2**53-1.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add `recent_session_logs` (src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:377, returns list[TicketStateOut]) to the affected-tools inventory and confirm the fix seam and regression test cover every TicketStateOut-returning call site — verified via find_referencing_symbols on TicketStateOut plus a string grep for TicketStateOut.
evidence: Plan: 'src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py — list_tickets / show_ticket / ready_tickets return those models.'
Plan: 'Tools whose models carry no ticket timestamps (search, summary, ticket_deps, explain_criterion, grounding_info) emit 0 and do not fail — a split that predicts exactly which tools break.'

src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:377-382: `def recent_session_logs(limit: int = 5) -> list[TicketStateOut]: ... return [TicketStateOut.model_validate(t) for t in rebar.recent_session_logs(limit=limit)]` — a fourth TicketStateOut-returning tool the plan's 'exactly which tools break' split omits.
findings.finding: The inventory of tools that emit ticket timestamps via `TicketStateOut` is incomplete: it names `list_tickets` / `show_ticket` / `ready_tickets` and claims to 'predict exactly which tools break', but `recent_session_logs` is a fourth call site of `TicketStateOut` (`src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:377`, returning `list[TicketStateOut]` from `rebar.recent_session_logs`) that passes the same undeclared `created_at`/`updated_at` `time.time_ns()` integers through the identical seam and would break identically.
findings.location: Root cause -> 'src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py -- list_tickets / show_ticket / ready_tickets return those models' and 'a split that predicts exactly which tools break'
scenarios: recent_session_logs (src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:377) returns list[TicketStateOut] with the same created_at/updated_at time_ns ints; if the fix's seam is scoped only to the three named tools it under-delivers and recent_session_logs keeps emitting bare 19-digit integers -> unpatched call site, still throws BigInt under a lossless JS client.
The regression-test AC names only list_tickets and ready_tickets, so a guard scoped by that inventory leaves recent_session_logs untested -> missed test coverage for an equally-affected tool.
findings.suggested_fix: In the root-cause 'which tools break' list and the fix scope, include recent_session_logs alongside list_tickets/show_ticket/ready_tickets (all four return TicketStateOut), and either extend an AC to cover it or state why its lower call frequency doesn't need one.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Require the LIVE VALIDATION JS client to be one with a lossless (BigInt-yielding) JSON parse (e.g. the Copilot CLI wasm-bindgen bridge that produced the original error), so 'no error' actually distinguishes fixed from broken.
evidence: Plan root cause: 'plain JSON.parse → the value silently truncates (no error)' vs 'a lossless parser (GitHub Copilot CLI ...) → yields a BigInt ... throws'
The AC phrasing 'through a JS client ... with no BigInt serialization error' is satisfied by ANY plain-JSON.parse client regardless of whether the fix shipped, because such a client never throws
findings.finding: The LIVE VALIDATION acceptance criteria do not pin that the validating JS client must be one whose LOSSLESS parse would have surfaced the original BigInt error; a plain-JSON.parse client would pass 'no BigInt serialization error' even against the still-broken build (it silently truncates rather than throwing).
findings.location: Acceptance criteria → LIVE VALIDATION → 'returns through a JS client ... with no BigInt serialization error'
scenarios: Live validation is run with a plain-JSON.parse JS client against a build where the guard did not deploy; the AC passes despite the data still being silently corrupted / the bug unfixed
findings.suggested_fix: Amend the two live-validation criteria to name the client (or class of client) whose lossless parse reproduced the original TypeError, and require the recorded response to show the timestamp value round-trips exactly (int(wire)==stored) rather than only 'no error'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Explicitly acknowledge the timestamp wire-type change (number -> decimal string) for MCP consumers and state the back-out/rollback path (or justify why no MCP consumer relies on the numeric type).
evidence: 'emit an integer outside the JS-safe range as its exact decimal string, so int(wire_value) == stored_value'
'CLI --output json and the Python library are unchanged' (MCP consumers not addressed)
findings.finding: The fix changes the JSON wire TYPE of timestamp fields from number to string for MCP consumers (so clients must int()-parse), which is a consumer-facing contract change for any MCP JS client that currently reads these as numbers. The plan states CLI --output json and the Python library are unchanged, but does not explicitly acknowledge the number->string change as a breaking-shape change for MCP consumers, nor a rollback/back-out path.
scenarios: An existing MCP client that does arithmetic on created_at/updated_at as a number would break when it now receives a string.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence noting the MCP seam changes affected timestamps to decimal strings, that this supersedes the previously-corrupting numeric emission, and describe how to revert (single-seam guard is toggleable/removable).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the MCP wire-contract change explicitly (out-of-range int timestamps become JSON strings for ALL MCP clients) and either document the schema-type change or add coverage/rationale for a non-JS remote-MCP consumer so the fix does not break another supported harness shape.
evidence: 'emit an integer outside the JS-safe range as its exact decimal string'
Matrix cell: Harness = 'remote MCP'
'CLI --output json and the Python library are unchanged' — but the MCP wire type change applies to all MCP clients regardless of language
findings.finding: The fix emits out-of-range integer timestamps as decimal STRINGS on the MCP wire, but only JS MCP clients are named in the acceptance criteria. A non-JS remote-MCP consumer that deserializes tool results into a typed model expecting an integer created_at/updated_at would now receive a string, changing the field's JSON type for every MCP client, not only the JS one that threw.
findings.location: Root cause — 'Fix shape: at the MCP tool-return seam only, emit an integer outside the JS-safe range as its exact decimal string'
scenarios: A non-JS remote-MCP client (Harness=remote MCP) that decodes list_tickets results into a schema with an integer-typed created_at receives a JSON string and fails deserialization or type-validation — an observable breakage not covered by the JS-only acceptance criteria.
A client that reads created_at as a number for sorting/comparison now sees a string and sorts lexicographically or errors.

findings.checklist_item: State the consumer-side contract of the number→string wire change: which fields become strings, confirm the named JS clients (Copilot CLI, Claude Code) tolerate a string timestamp, and add an AC that verifies a consumer reads the value back correctly (not merely that no error is thrown).
evidence: Plan: 'emit an integer outside the JS-safe range as its exact decimal string, so int(wire_value) == stored_value with no rounding'
The AC set only verifies 'no serialization error' and 'returns a ticket list' — none verify that a consumer still interprets the timestamp correctly after the number→string change
